titleEn: The voice of the LORD over the waters
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm C | Dm Dm |
intro: Eleven verses and a thunderstorm crossing the country from the sea to the southern desert. The phrase to learn is the one that opens seven of the lines, the voice of the LORD, because it is a construct chain, two nouns welded into one unit with no word for of between them, which is how Hebrew builds most of its possessives. Count the divine name while you read: it appears eighteen times in eleven verses, and seven of those stand at the head of a line inside that same phrase. Said on Friday night at the close of Kabbalat Shabbat, and in the Ashkenazi rite while the Torah scroll is carried back to the ark on Shabbat morning.

stichs.en: A psalm of David.
Give to the LORD, you divine beings,
give to the LORD glory and strength.

verses.summary: The psalm opens above the weather, in a heavenly court that is told twice in one verse to hand something over. Nothing has been given to the singer yet.

stichs.en: Give to the LORD the glory of His name,
bow down to the LORD in the splendour of holiness.

verses.summary: The third and last imperative to give, followed by the one thing a court cannot manufacture: bowing. Worship is the protocol of the room, not its furniture.

stichs.en: The voice of the LORD is over the waters,
the God of glory thunders,
the LORD over many waters.

verses.summary: The storm arrives and the formula that will run seven times through the psalm is heard for the first time. The water here is the sea, not the rain.

stichs.en: The voice of the LORD is in power,
the voice of the LORD is in majesty.

verses.summary: Two clauses, no verb in either one, and the shortest line pair in the psalm. Hebrew uses a preposition where English insists on the word is.

stichs.en: The voice of the LORD breaks cedars,
and the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon.

verses.summary: The first casualty is the tallest tree in the region. The root for breaking is used twice, first as a participle and then as an intensive, so it happens and then happens harder.

stichs.en: He makes them skip like a calf,
Lebanon and Sirion like a young wild ox.

verses.summary: Now the mountains move. A range that was being smashed a line ago is a calf jumping, and the violence turns into something closer to dancing without ever stopping.

stichs.en: The voice of the LORD hews out flames of fire.

verses.summary: The one verse with no second half, sitting at the centre of the seven. Lightning, described with the verb of a stonecutter rather than of a weapon.

stichs.en: The voice of the LORD makes the wilderness writhe,
the LORD makes the wilderness of Kadesh writhe.

verses.summary: The storm has crossed the whole map, north to south. Kadesh is desert, so the voice is now shaking a place with nothing left in it to break.

stichs.en: The voice of the LORD sends the hinds into labour
and strips the forests bare,
and in His temple all of it says: Glory.

verses.summary: The seventh and last voice, and the move indoors. Outside, cover is being torn off; inside, everything says the single word the heavenly court was ordered to hand over in verse 1.

stichs.en: The LORD sat enthroned at the flood,
and the LORD sits as king for ever.

verses.summary: Two verbs of sitting close the storm off. The water of verse 3 is named as the flood, and the one who was seated before it began is still seated after.

stichs.en: The LORD will give strength to His people,
the LORD will bless His people with peace.

verses.summary: Strength comes back from verse 1, moving downward this time. What the court above was told to give is handed to the people below, and the psalm ends on a word it has not used once: peace.

pardes.body: A storm crosses the map. It starts over the water at {{3.0}}, breaks the cedars of Lebanon in the north at verse 5, and shakes the wilderness of Kadesh in the south at verse 8, and the phrase the voice of the LORD stands at the head of a line seven times. The frame is what makes it a psalm and not a weather report: verses 1 and 2 are set in a heavenly court, verses 10 and 11 in the temple and among the people, and the last word is peace. Everything violent happens between two rooms where nothing moves.

Three places where the Hebrew is contested. {{1.5}} is either divine beings, members of a heavenly court, or mighty ones, human nobles, and the choice decides whether verse 1 is addressed to angels or to men. {{9.3}} is normally read as hinds, so the voice sends the deer into labour, but the parallel half-line strips the forests at {{9.5}}, and the same consonants can be read as a word for oaks, which would make both halves about trees. Sirion at {{6.4}} is not a puzzle: Deuteronomy 3:9 states that Sirion is what the Sidonians called Mount Hermon, so verse 6 names the same range twice under two names.

The very last line of the Mishnah, at the end of tractate Uktzin, takes verse 11 as its closing proof text: the Holy One found no vessel that holds blessing for Israel except peace, as it says, the LORD will bless His people with peace. That is the traditional answer to why a psalm of thunder ends quietly, and it is why {{11.8}} carries more weight than its position suggests. One reading hears the seven voices as the voice at Sinai, and on that reading the wilderness of verse 8 is not scenery but the place where the Torah was given.

In kabbalistic reading the seven voices are the seven lower sefirot, the channels through which the world is built and unbuilt, which is why one voice can break cedars and another can hand over peace. The Safed kabbalists of the sixteenth century built the Friday night service out of six psalms, one for each weekday, and placed this one last, so the week ends on the psalm of seven voices and Shabbat enters on the word at {{11.8}}. The divine name appears eighteen times here, and eighteen is the number written in Hebrew letters as chai, life.
